extraction_supporting_text.exposure_measurement: serum levels of the major vitamin D metabolites, 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-D3) and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25-D)

sample_size.excerpt: Among black men in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial, we identified 226 prostate cancer cases and 452 controls matched on age at randomization (±5 years), date of blood draw (±30 days), calendar year of cohort entry, and time since baseline prostate cancer screening (±1 year).
sample_size.location: Abstract, sentence 2; total_n derived from reported group counts 226 + 452 = 678

cases.excerpt: Among black men in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial, we identified 226 prostate cancer cases and 452 controls matched on age at randomization (±5 years), date of blood draw (±30 days), calendar year of cohort entry, and time since baseline prostate cancer screening (±1 year).

effect_size.excerpt: Serum 25(OH)D was not associated with overall prostate cancer (Q4 vs Q1: OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.40-1.33; P for trend = .25), although there were apparent inverse associations for nonaggressive disease (global P = .03, clinical stage I/II, and Gleason score <7) and among men ≥62 years old (P for interaction = .04) that were restricted to Q3. Interestingly, serum DBP was significantly inversely associated with prostate cancer risk (Q4 vs Q1: OR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.20-1.00; P for trend = .03), whereas the 25(OH)D:DBP molar ratio was not.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Serum 25(OH)D was not associated with overall prostate cancer (Q4 vs Q1: OR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.40-1.33; P for trend = .25), although there were apparent inverse associations for nonaggressive disease (global P = .03, clinical stage I/II, and Gleason score <7) and among men ≥62 years old (P for interaction = .04) that were restricted to Q3.

sample_size.excerpt: After exclusions, our analytic sample consisted of 227,890 non-Hispanic men: 221,032 white and 6858 black.

cases.excerpt: During a median of 15.5 years of follow-up, 28,845 incident prostate cancers were identified in white men (3898 advanced), and 1417 in black men (209 advanced).

effect_size.excerpt: Q1 white men = 1.14, 95% CI:1.06–1.23, P trend = 0.0001; black men HR = 0.73, 95% CI:0.49–1.07, P trend = 0.18; P interaction = 0.02). Tests for interactions between race and supplemental or supplemental plus dietary vitamin D intake did not reach statistical significance (data not shown), nor was there evidence of interaction with any of the other evaluated factors ( Supplementary Table 2 ).

evidence_scope_projection.definition: Overall prostate cancer evidence, excluding estimates solely about aggressive prostate cancer. General estimates from papers that also report aggressive endpoints remain included. Uncertain endpoints retain their existing review and pooling restrictions.

headline.funnel_interpretation: The significant funnel plot asymmetry (egger's p=0.0164) indicates substantial publication bias in this meta-analysis on Vitamin D and prostate cancer\aggressive. This specific pattern suggests that smaller studies with smaller or null effects may be underrepresented, compromising the reliability of the pooled estimate and potentially leading to an overestimation of the true association.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 26 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.14 (95% CI: 1.08–1.2), suggesting that Vitamin D is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer\aggressive. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 71.86%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
